fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak “…rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:2) The prophets spoke, and these two got moving. Work boots on.

Not this time, friend. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak did the opposite of leaving. The text says they “…rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:2) Packing a suitcase while the prophets are still echoing would be a bold move.

I can see why you'd think so, but the text says something different. “…the prophets of God were with them, helping them.” (Ezra 5:2) The prophets didn't head home once the building started. They were with the builders, helping them.

That's right, baker. The text says the elders “…were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.” (Ezra 5:5) The governor asked his questions, and the elders were not stopped. A governor shows up with questions, and still they aren't stopped.

That's right. “…the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews…” (Ezra 5:5) That's why they weren't stopped. A governor was asking questions, and God's eye was on them. The text doesn't say anything fancy about how, only that His eye was on them.

Haggai is one of the prophets who prophesied to the Jews, and the prophets were with the builders, helping them. (Ezra 5:1-2) But the eye on the elders belongs to someone else. “…the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews…” (Ezra 5:5) That's the reason they weren't stopped.

Yes, baker. The elders answer, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth…” (Ezra 5:11) Tattenai had asked who authorized the rebuilding, and this is how they begin their answer. Not a title, not a name drop, just who they serve.

Darius is the king Tattenai is writing to (Ezra 5:6), so it's an understandable guess. But the elders never call themselves his servants. They say, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth…” (Ezra 5:11)
Jeshua is a priest in this story (Ezra 3:2), so it's a fair guess. But the elders don't call the builder that. They say it was “…a great king of Israel built and completed.” (Ezra 5:11)

Darius is the king Tattenai writes to (Ezra 5:6), so his name is easy to grab. But the elders point back to an earlier king. “In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.” (Ezra 5:13) It's Cyrus who issued the decree.

You got it, baker. Cyrus gave the gold and silver articles “…to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor” (Ezra 5:14) A governor's title and all those gold and silver articles. That's a lot to get from Cyrus, Sheshbazzar.

It does say that. The elders quote Cyrus telling Sheshbazzar, “Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.” (Ezra 5:15) So Cyrus's instruction names the original site. The place was part of the instruction.

Doors aren't mentioned in this part of the story. The elders say Sheshbazzar “…came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem…” (Ezra 5:16) The foundation is what he laid. Hanging doors before the foundation is down would be like stamping a cookie before the dough is even mixed.

Yes, baker. Tattenai writes, “…let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:17) He wants it checked in the records. He's asking for the search, then waiting on the king's decision. If the king says yes, somebody gets a dusty job.

Good guess for a governor's letter, but it's not the word. Tattenai writes, “…let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon…” (Ezra 5:17) He's asking for the records to be searched. This passage ends with the request.
